# AGENTS.md

Instructions for coding agents working on this repository. [README.md](README.md) explains what the plugin does and
what opencode taught us; [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) is the guide for human contributors.

## The project

An opencode plugin (v1 plugin API, opencode `>=1.18.29 <2`) that makes read-only agents (`plan`, `explore`, agents
with `edit: deny`) actually read-only: it parses every shell command and refuses writes before opencode's permission
check, injects the shared allowlist from `rules/` into those agents, and logs their prompts for a reviewed learning
step. The command-line tool `opencode-readonly-guard` exposes the same decisions.

## Commands

Tool versions are pinned in `mise.toml` (bun, node, hk, actionlint, shellcheck, opencode). Run from the repository root.

| Command                     | What it does                                                                       |
| --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `mise run setup`            | `bun install --frozen-lockfile` and the hk git hooks (shared by all worktrees)     |
| `mise run check`            | lint, fmt:check, typecheck and test: what CI runs; must pass before every commit   |
| `mise run lint`             | `oxlint --deny-warnings`                                                           |
| `mise run fmt`              | `prettier --write .`; `fmt:check` only checks (Markdown and JSON included)         |
| `mise run typecheck`        | `tsc --noEmit` over `src/` and `test/`                                             |
| `mise run test`             | unit tests (`bun test test/unit`); one file: `bun test test/unit/analyze.test.ts`  |
| `mise run build`            | bundle `src/` into `dist/` (plugin and CLI, zod included; read the hazards first)  |
| `mise run test:integration` | build, then drive the real opencode without a model and install the packed tarball |
| `mise run test:e2e`         | build, then drive a real model with your credentials; costs money, only when asked |

No build needed: `bun src/cli.ts check --no-store '<command>'` prints what a read-only agent gets (allow, ask or block)
under the shared rules, and `bun src/cli.ts vet '<pattern>'` runs the safety check that learned patterns go through.

## Code style

- TypeScript `strict`, `module`/`moduleResolution` NodeNext, ES2023. Relative imports end in `.js`, type-only imports
  use `import type` (`verbatimModuleSyntax`), Node built-ins the `node:` prefix.
- prettier: no semicolons, 120 columns, 2 spaces. oxlint denies warnings; `any` and `console` are errors.
- `src/index.ts` keeps a single default export: opencode calls every export of a plugin module as a plugin.
- Every behaviour change comes with a unit test; comments say why, not what.

## Map

`src/`

- `index.ts`: the module's only export, `{ id, server }`.
- `plugin.ts`: the opencode hooks: `config` (inject the rules, register `/guard-review`), `tool.execute.before` (the
  write guard), `event` (log prompts and answers), `chat.params` (which agent owns a session). Every hook returns at
  once unless its copy is in charge. `copies.ts`: how copies of the plugin in one opencode instance (a global and a
  project entry) agree that the one loaded last runs; a new hook must check `copy.active()` too. A copy that fails in
  its config hook, or cannot read its rules even from the built-in copy, fails closed (`failClosed` in `inject.ts`)
  unless a copy that started is in charge.
- `shell.ts`: POSIX-ish tokenizer (simple commands, redirections, substitutions); what it cannot parse is blocked.
- `analyze.ts`: the write guard: redirections, wrappers, `sed -i`, `find -delete`, git and package-manager writes, …
  `environment.ts`: statements that export variables to later commands (`export`, `set -a`, namerefs, a new value
  for an exported variable) or list them all (`export -p`), which opencode never prompts for. `programs.ts`: its
  argument parsers for system tools (systemctl, journalctl, ip, mount, pacman, docker/podman, virsh, lspci, ss, xxd,
  ps), which follow each program's own option rules (abbreviations, bundles, values).
- `wildcard.ts`: opencode's pattern matching, last match wins. `decide.ts`: allow, ask or block for a command line,
  over the stages opencode builds a pattern for (`simpleCommands` in `shell.ts`).
- `rules.ts`: loads `rules/*.json` and builds the ordered bash rule list, ending with the help layer (exact
  `<program> <subcommand> --help` and `git help <subcommand>` commands) and the redirection twins (`<exact rule> 2>&1`,
  `2>/dev/null`). A file that cannot be read is replaced by the copy `embed.ts` builds in (a Bun macro: `bun build`
  and `bun` itself replace its call with the files' text). `inject.ts`: finds the read-only agents and writes their
  rules into opencode's config.
- `classify.ts`: the safety check for patterns (learned rules, the `allow` option, `vet`).
- `sources.ts`: presets (`herdr-ui`) and the merge of options, store and herdr's file. `options.ts`: plugin options
  and default paths.
- `store.ts`: learned rules (`readonly-guard.json`). `log.ts`: the event log (`events.jsonl`, rotated).
- `review.ts`, `tools.ts`, `command.ts`: the log summary, the `readonly_guard_review` and `readonly_guard_update`
  tools, the `/guard-review` command.
- `commands.ts`, `cli.ts`: the command-line tool. `doctor.ts`: its `doctor` subcommand (runs `opencode debug config`
  through `CliIo.exec`). `constants.ts`: ids and tool names.

`rules/`: `allow.json`, `ask.json`, `commands.json`, `cases.json` and their JSON Schemas in `schema/` (CONTRIBUTING.md
describes each file). They ship in the npm package and are read at runtime; `dist/` also carries a copy from build
time, used only when a file cannot be read.

`test/`

- `unit/`: mostly one file per module. `cases.test.ts` runs every case in `rules/cases.json`; `rules.test.ts` checks
  the rule files against each other.
- `integration/`: the real opencode without a model (`opencode debug config|agent` in a sandbox project), two copies
  of the plugin in one opencode, copies with corrupt rule files, `doctor`, and the packed tarball. Broken copies are
  `file://` copies of the build (`copyPlugin()`); never put an unpublished npm name in a config, opencode would
  install whatever the registry serves under it.
- `e2e/`: a real model drives a read-only harness agent; opt-in (`OPENCODE_E2E=1`, set by the mise task).
- `helpers.ts`: `sandbox()`, a throwaway project with its own XDG directories, store and log (and, with
  `globalPlugin`, its own global config). Use it for anything that starts opencode. `childEnv()`: the caller's
  environment without `GIT_*` and `HERDR_*`, for any other child process (see "Hazards").

`memory/sessions/`: redacted transcripts of the maintainer's work sessions: history, not documentation. Its README.md
has the naming and the export procedure; prettier and the whitespace hooks skip it (`.prettierignore`, `hk.pkl`), and
it is not in the npm package. See "State, scratch and transcripts".

## Changing the rules

Follow "Adding a command to the allowlist" in [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md); do not work from memory. A rule
change and its cases in `rules/cases.json` go in the same commit. `/add-rule <command>` walks through it.

## opencode in this repository

- `opencode.json` lets agents run the check tasks (`mise run check|lint|fmt|fmt:check|typecheck|test`, `bun test`),
  the read-only CLI subcommands and read-only `git` and `gh` commands without a prompt, plus their `rtk …` forms for
  the rtk plugin. Everything else asks, including `mise run build`, `setup`, the integration and e2e tests, `:::` task
  lists and `--output`. Widen it in your own config, not here.
- `.opencode/commands/`: `/check` (run `mise run check`, fix or report) and `/add-rule <command>`.
- `"plugin": ["."]` loads the plugin from this checkout's own `dist/` (dogfooding): a session started in a checkout
  or worktree is guarded by that checkout's build, see "Hazards". Without a build the entry is skipped without a
  word. In read-only agents (`plan`, `explore`) the plugin's rules come after the `permission` block above, so its
  `"*": "ask"` wins there: only the shared allowlist runs without a prompt, and the check tasks, `bun src/cli.ts` and
  `gh` ask; `build` keeps them. If you also configure the plugin globally, the project's entry is in charge here and
  its options (none) replace your global entry's options. `bun src/cli.ts doctor` shows which copy guards a
  directory (`test/integration/dogfood.test.ts` pins all of this).

## State, scratch and transcripts

- An agent keeps its durable state (notes, helper scripts) in `.state/<agent>/` and disposable scratch in
  `.state/<agent>/tmp/`. Both are ignored by git, never published, and private to that agent. `.tmp/` is ignored too.
- Nothing durable in `/tmp`: it is cleaned after days and lost at reboots.
- `git clean -X` and `git clean -fdx` delete ignored files, `.state/` included: not in a checkout whose state you keep.
- A sandbox that runs git or opencode (outside the tests, which use `sandbox()`) needs its own git root (`git init`),
  or they take the enclosing checkout as the project.
- Never commit a raw session export. Transcripts go to `memory/sessions/` redacted, by the procedure in its README.md:
  the repository is public, and what is committed cannot be unpublished.

## Dependency updates

Renovate (`renovate.json`) opens grouped weekly pull requests for npm and `bun.lock`, `mise.toml` (opencode included),
`hk.pkl` and the GitHub Actions; see "Dependency updates" in CONTRIBUTING.md. A pull request that bumps opencode or
`@opencode-ai/plugin` is ready only when `mise run test:integration` passes.

## Commits

- [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org), checked by hk's `commit-msg` hook; follow the format by
  hand where the hooks are not installed. Scope by module or area, as in `git log`: `feat(rules)`, `fix(analyze)`,
  `test(integration)`, `docs(todo)`, `build(mise)`, `ci(github)`.
- One logical change per commit. Run `mise run check` before committing.
- User-visible changes (rules, options, CLI, behaviour) get a line in `CHANGELOG.md` under "Unreleased"; repository
  tooling does not.

## Hazards

- **`dist/` is live.** It is gitignored build output, and opencode loads it from any checkout that a config names as
  `file:///path/to/checkout`, this repository's own `opencode.json` included (`"."`, the checkout it sits in).
  `mise run build`, and every task that depends on it (`test:integration`, `test:e2e`, `pack`), replaces the plugin
  for every opencode session that starts afterwards with that checkout configured: the sessions started in that
  checkout, and every directory whose config names it (a global `file://` entry to the main checkout). Sessions
  already running keep the copy they loaded. Build in your own clone or worktree, never in a checkout that other
  sessions load. Unit tests and `bun src/cli.ts` do not need `dist/`.
- **A worktree's build guards that worktree.** Its sessions load its `dist/`, work in progress included, and that
  copy is in charge over a global entry to the main checkout (the project's entry is loaded last). A build there
  only reaches sessions started in that worktree, but a build that loads and misbehaves (blocks too much, asks for
  nothing) misguards them; `bun src/cli.ts doctor` names the copy in charge. While the worktree has no `dist/` (never
  built, or a session starting mid-build: the build deletes it first), its entry is skipped without a word and the
  global copy guards it, or nothing does without one. A worktree built before copies agreed on one (#8) runs next to
  the global copy: rebuild it.
- **Never touch the user's real store, log or config.** By default the plugin reads `readonly-guard.json` and writes
  `events.jsonl` under the XDG directories. Tests go through `sandbox()`, or set `READONLY_GUARD_STORE` and
  `READONLY_GUARD_DATA` to temporary paths. The same goes for running opencode by hand: `opencode debug config` loads
  every globally configured plugin, including an installed copy of this one, which then writes to its log.
- **Tests run inside git hooks.** The pre-push hook runs the unit tests with git's hook environment: in a linked
  worktree git exports `GIT_DIR=<main>/.git/worktrees/<name>`, and hk adds `GIT_WORK_TREE`. A test that starts git
  with the inherited environment acts on the worker's repository, wherever its `cwd`: `git init` in a temporary
  directory wrote `core.bare` or `core.worktree` into the shared `.git/config` (`git status` in the main checkout then
  shows the worktree's files), and `git commit` committed on the worker's branch. Start git, opencode and anything
  that may run git through `sandbox()`, or pass `env: childEnv()` (`test/helpers.ts`), which drops every `GIT_*`.

# opencode-readonly-guard

Make opencode's read-only agents (`plan`, `explore`, and any agent with `edit: deny`) actually read-only.

In opencode, "plan mode" is a request to the model, not a restriction: the `plan` and `explore` agents can run any
shell command, so a model that ignores the reminder can still `rm`, `sed -i` or `> file`. This plugin closes that gap:

- **Write guard.** Before opencode evaluates any permission rule, the full command line is parsed and refused if it
  writes: redirections in any position, `tee` to a file, `rm`/`cp`/`mv`/…, `sed -i`, `git commit`, `npm install`,
  `find -delete`, `curl -o`, and wrappers around them (`sudo`, `env`, `xargs`, `bash -c`, `$(…)`). It also refuses
  to export environment variables to the commands that follow and to list every variable (`export -p`, `declare`),
  which opencode never prompts for, and the `ps` forms that print process environments (`ps e`, `-o environ`). The
  model gets an error that tells it to return the data in its reply instead.
- **Shared allowlist.** Read-only agents ask before running anything except a vetted list of read-only commands
  (`ls`, `cat`, `rg`, `sort`, `echo`, `sha256sum`, `readlink -f`, `ps aux`, `ss -tlnp`, `git log`, `git branch -a`,
  `git describe`, `systemctl status`, `docker ps`, `ip addr`, `herdr agent list`, …). The list lives in
  [`rules/`](rules) as plain JSON that anyone can extend.
- **Reviewed learning.** An "always" answer in a read-only agent is only logged as a candidate. `/guard-review` shows
  candidates with safe pattern options, and a rule is added only after you confirm the exact pattern.
- **Event log.** Every shell command, block, prompt and answer in a read-only agent is recorded, so the policy can be
  improved with data.

Tested with opencode 1.19.3 (supported range `>=1.18.29 <2`). opencode 2.x has a different plugin API and is not
supported yet, see [TODO.md](TODO.md).

## Install

```sh
opencode plugin opencode-readonly-guard --global   # adds it to ~/.config/opencode/opencode.json
```

or add it to your config by hand, with options if you want them:

```jsonc
// opencode.json
{
  "plugin": [
    "opencode-readonly-guard",
    // or: ["opencode-readonly-guard", { "agents": { "include": ["reviewer"] }, "allow": ["uptime *"] }]
  ],
}
```

Restart opencode afterwards (config and plugins are loaded once at startup).

Other ways:

| Tool        | Command                                                                           |
| ----------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| npm / bun   | `npm i -g opencode-readonly-guard` · `bun add -g opencode-readonly-guard`         |
| mise (CLI)  | `mise use -g npm:opencode-readonly-guard`                                         |
| From source | `git clone … && mise run setup build`, then `"plugin": ["file:///path/to/clone"]` |

> The package is not published to npm yet (see [TODO.md](TODO.md)). Until then, use the from-source route. A session
> started inside the clone loads its build anyway, through the repository's own config (see [Development](#development)).

Configured more than once (a global and a project entry, or two checkouts), the plugin runs once: the copy loaded
last is in charge and the others stay passive. opencode loads the global config before the project's, so the
project's entry wins, and its options replace the global entry's (they are not merged). The `init` event in the log
names the copy in charge (`module`) and every copy loaded (`copies`). A copy built before this rule does not know
about it and still runs next to the others.

The build carries a copy of `rules/*.json`. A rule file that cannot be read (corrupt, missing) is replaced by that
copy, so read-only agents keep the full policy and the write guard; an `error` event (`where: "rules"`) names the
file, the `init` event lists it under `builtin`, and a warning toast says so. A file that reads fine is always used,
so editing the rules of a checkout needs no build. If the plugin still cannot start (an error while it applies the
rules), it fails closed: read-only agents ask before every shell command (their own deny rules stay), the write guard
stays on, an `error` event names the reason and a toast says so. These toasts are shown whatever the `toast` option.
A copy that started, loaded before or after a broken one, is in charge instead, and its `init` event lists the broken
copy under `failed`. A plugin that opencode cannot even import (a checkout without `dist/`) runs no code and cannot
report anything: run `opencode-readonly-guard doctor` in the project to check.

## Using it

**`/guard-review`** (registered by the plugin, runs in `build`) summarizes the log: blocked commands, the most-prompted
commands and allowlist candidates. For each candidate you pick the exact rule to keep (the exact command, the same
command limited to its directory, or opencode's general pattern, whichever the safety check accepts) or dismiss it.
opencode then asks you to confirm that exact pattern before it is written to `readonly-guard.json`. New rules apply
after a restart. In read-only agents the review tools are hidden, so an agent cannot extend its own allowlist.

**Command-line tool** (`opencode-readonly-guard`, also available as `npx opencode-readonly-guard`):

```text
check [--json] [--no-store] <command>   what a read-only agent gets: allow | ask | block (exit status 0 | 1 | 2)
vet <pattern>                           may this pattern be added to the allowlist?
rules [--json]                          print the shared allowlist and the always-ask flags
review [--limit N]                      print the log summary
install [-g] [--force]                  opencode plugin opencode-readonly-guard
doctor [--json]                         is the guard active here? (exit status 0 | 1)
```

```console
$ opencode-readonly-guard check 'git log --oneline | head'
allow
$ opencode-readonly-guard check 'ls | cat > notes.txt'
block  write redirection "> notes.txt"
$ opencode-readonly-guard check 'uptime'
ask    needs approval: uptime
```

`doctor` starts opencode in the current directory without a model (`opencode debug config`, the plugin's log for that
run goes to a temporary directory) and reports: this plugin's entries in the config and which one is in charge, why a
`file://` copy cannot be imported (`dist/index.js is missing: a checkout that was not built, run mise run build in
…`), whether opencode's version is in each entry's `engines.opencode` range, which agents carry the guard's rules and
how many, the errors of that start (a rule file replaced by the built-in copy is a warning), and the last start
logged for the project. It exits with 1 when the guard is not active, including when it failed closed; `--json`
prints the report.

## How the policy is built

For every read-only agent the plugin writes this ordered bash rule list into the config (the last matching rule wins):

1. `"*": ask`
2. the shared allowlist, [`rules/allow.json`](rules/allow.json)
3. presets that are on (see [Working inside herdr](#working-inside-herdr)), learned rules (`readonly-guard.json`) and
   the `allow` option, each re-checked at startup
4. the agent's own bash rules, if it had any
5. the always-ask flags, [`rules/ask.json`](rules/ask.json): `find -delete/-exec`, `rg --pre`, `git … --output`,
   `sort --compress-program`, `git ls-remote --upload-pack`, …
6. the help layer: exact `<program> <subcommand> --help` commands for git, herdr, npm and mise (`git commit --help`,
   `herdr worktree create --help`) and `git help <subcommand>`, derived from
   [`rules/commands.json`](rules/commands.json). They only print help; the layer holds no wildcard, never covers an
   ask-listed flag, and never overrides a deny or an exact rule of the agent's own.
7. the redirection twins: `<command> 2>&1` and `<command> 2>/dev/null` for every exact command allowed above
   (`herdr --help 2>&1`), because opencode matches a command together with its redirections. A twin is only added
   where no rule but `*` matches it, so it never overrides an ask flag, a deny or an agent's own rule.

Because the flags come after every allow rule, a broad learned rule such as `find *` never silences `find . -delete`.

Some commands are only allowed in their read-only forms, because the bare subcommand writes: `git branch` lists, but
`git branch NAME` creates a branch, so the allowlist has `git branch`, `git branch -a *`, `git branch --contains*`, …
and the write guard blocks the creating forms. System tools follow the same idea: `ip addr *` is allowed because the
guard resolves every verb abbreviation iproute2 accepts and blocks `add`, `set`, `flush`, …; `docker ps *` because
docker only takes `-H`/`--context` before the subcommand, where no rule matches. `git config KEY`, `git -C DIR …`
and commands behind an environment prefix (`LC_ALL=C sort`) still ask.

Read-only agents are `plan`, `explore`, every agent whose `permission.edit` is `deny` (or `tools.edit: false`), plus
`agents.include`, minus `agents.exclude`. `plan` additionally asks before delegating to a subagent that is not
read-only, and never to `general`.

## Working inside herdr

Agents that run in a [herdr](https://herdr.dev) pane can inspect it with the `herdr` CLI. The rules treat `herdr` like
`git`: they judge the subcommand, never the program as a whole (`herdr *` is never accepted).

- **Allowed without a prompt:** `--help`, `--version`, `--skill`, a bare command group (`herdr agent`, `herdr pane`, …)
  and the read-only subcommands: `status`, `agent list|get|read|wait|explain`,
  `pane list|current|get|layout|process-info|neighbor|edges|read|wait-output`, `workspace|tab list|get`,
  `worktree|session|machine|plugin|integration` listings, `api snapshot|schema`, `config check`, `channel show`.
  Also `herdr <subcommand> --help` exactly, for every subcommand below except the UI ones
  (`herdr worktree create --help`): it only prints help.
- **Always asks**, even when an agent's own rules allow `herdr *`, and can never be learned (exact or with a wildcard):
  every other subcommand, such as `pane send-text|send-keys|run|split|close`, `agent prompt|send-keys|start`,
  `tab|workspace create|close|focus`, `server stop`, `session stop`. A read-only agent must not send instructions to
  another agent, so `agent prompt` stays a prompt. The `--machine`, `--session` and `--remote` prefixes, bare `herdr`
  (it opens the terminal UI) and `--trust-repository` ask too.
- **Blocked** like other writes: `herdr update`, `worktree create|remove`, `config reset-keys`,
  `integration install|uninstall`, `session delete`, `plugin install|update`, `api schema --output FILE`, and
  `pane run PANE CMD` when `CMD` would itself be blocked (`herdr pane run w1:p2 'rm -rf build'`).
- **UI commands, on inside herdr:** `herdr tab rename` and `herdr notification show` only change what herdr
  displays, which is how a plan-mode agent can report its state. They are the `herdr-ui` preset: allowed without a
  prompt when opencode runs in a herdr pane (`HERDR_ENV=1`), and not otherwise. Outside a pane the herdr CLI still
  reaches the running session and acts on whatever is focused there, so a UI command listed in your store or options
  is ignored outside herdr too. The preset is built into the plugin and is not part of the shared allowlist.

  Switch it off with `"presets": { "herdr-ui": false }`, and list the one command you want instead:

  ```jsonc
  // ~/.config/opencode/readonly-guard.json (the store), or in the plugin options,
  // or in herdr's own directory: ~/.config/herdr/readonly-guard.json
  { "presets": { "herdr-ui": false }, "allow": ["herdr tab rename *"] }
  ```

  Where the settings come from:

  | Source                                  | Keys                    | Notes                                                       |
  | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------- |
  | plugin options in `opencode.json`       | `presets`, `allow`      | lowest precedence                                           |
  | the store `readonly-guard.json`         | `presets`, `allow`, ... | the file `/guard-review` writes                             |
  | `readonly-guard.json` in herdr's config | `presets`, `allow`      | read only inside herdr, never written, wins over the others |

  herdr's directory is the one holding `$HERDR_CONFIG_PATH`, else `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/herdr` (`~/.config/herdr`). If
  sources disagree about a preset, the last in the table wins; `allow` lists add up. Every `allow` pattern passes the
  same safety check, so no file can allow `herdr agent prompt`, and herdr's file may only hold `herdr …` patterns.
  `opencode-readonly-guard vet 'herdr tab rename *'` shows what the safety check says about a pattern, and `check`
  follows the same rules as the plugin (`--no-store` means the shared rules only: no store, no presets).

herdr is not in opencode's table of known programs, so an "always" answer to any herdr prompt is saved by opencode as
`herdr *`, for every agent until restart. The write guard still blocks the commands above, but nothing stops
`herdr pane send-text`. Answer "once" to herdr prompts. rtk does not rewrite herdr commands, so there are no `rtk herdr`
rules.

## Options

Set them with the tuple form: `["opencode-readonly-guard", { … }]`.

| Option           | Default                                         | Meaning                                                         |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `agents.include` | `[]`                                            | extra agents to treat as read-only (they must exist)            |
| `agents.exclude` | `[]`                                            | agents to leave alone                                           |
| `allow`          | `[]`                                            | extra bash patterns to allow; each passes the same safety check |
| `presets`        | `{}`                                            | switch built-in rule sets on or off: `{ "herdr-ui": false }`    |
| `store`          | `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/opencode/readonly-guard.json` | learned rules, dismissed candidates, agent lists                |
| `logDir`         | `$XDG_DATA_HOME/opencode/readonly-guard`        | `events.jsonl` (rotated at 5 MB to `events.old.jsonl`)          |
| `toast`          | `true`                                          | warn when an "always" answer is given in a read-only agent      |
| `command`        | `"guard-review"`                                | name of the review command, or `false` to not register it       |

`READONLY_GUARD_STORE` and `READONLY_GUARD_DATA` override the default paths (an explicit option wins). The store file
is plain JSON and safe to keep in your dotfiles; the event log contains the commands your agents ran, so keep it local.
The startup `init` event in the log lists the `presets` in effect next to the number of `learned` rules, and the
copies of the plugin loaded or `failed`, and the rule files replaced by the built-in copy (`builtin`, see
[Install](#install)); a copy that fails closed logs an `error` event instead (`where`: `load` or `config`,
`writeGuard`: whether the write guard is still on).

## What it does not do

This is an accident preventer and a policy engine, not a sandbox.

- Only the `bash`/`shell` tool is covered. MCP tools, `webfetch` and others follow opencode's normal permissions.
- Interpreters can write (`python -c`, `node -e`, `awk`, `sqlite3 .shell`). They are not on the allowlist, so they
  prompt, but the guard does not read their code, and a broad "always" answer would let them through.
- Parsing is a hand-written approximation of POSIX shell; anything it cannot parse is blocked rather than guessed.
- Linux and macOS shells only. PowerShell is not parsed.
- "Always" answers made in opencode itself stay in effect for all agents until restart, see the findings below. The
  plugin warns, logs them and keeps the write guard on top, but it cannot revoke them.

## Findings about opencode 1.19.3

What building this taught us. Each point was checked against the binary or by a live run, and several are worth an
upstream issue (they are in [TODO.md](TODO.md)).

**Permissions**

- Plan mode is a prompt. The `plan` agent only denies the `edit` tool (except plan files); its `bash` is `* allow`
  and so is `explore`'s. The "READ-ONLY phase" text is a reminder injected into the conversation.
- Rules are evaluated in order and the last match wins; `*` matches anything and a trailing ` *` also matches the bare
  command.
- Bash commands are split with tree-sitter and each simple command is matched on its own text. That text includes a
  redirection only when the command's direct parent is the redirection, so `cat a > b` is matched as written, while
  the redirections of later pipeline stages (`a | b > f`), `{ …; } > f` and `( … ) > f` are invisible to patterns.
  Glob rules therefore cannot stop those writes; a parser in `tool.execute.before` can.
- Commands inside `$(…)`, backticks and `<(…)` are checked as separate commands.
- Only tree-sitter `command` nodes get a pattern, and `cd`, `chdir`, `pushd` and `popd` are skipped. Declarations
  (`export`, `declare`, `local`, `readonly`, `typeset`), `unset`, bare assignments (`B=/x`), `[ ]`, `[[ ]]` and
  `(( ))` never prompt, whatever they do: without the write guard, `export -p` prints the whole environment in plan
  mode unasked. The guard is the only check on them.

**"Always" answers**

- The saved pattern is the command prefix plus `*`, using a built-in table of how many words matter (`git log *`,
  `npm view *`) and falling back to the first word. Unknown programs become `prog *`: answering "always" to
  `tee /dev/null` allowed `tee *`, and for anything rewritten by the rtk plugin it is `rtk *`.
- It is kept in memory for the whole opencode process, is checked after every agent's rules (so it beats `ask` and
  `deny`), applies to all agents and sessions, and is lost on restart. The `permission` table in the database stays
  empty.

**Plugin API**

- `tool.execute.before` runs before the permission check; throwing from it aborts the tool call and the message reaches
  the model. This is what makes the write guard possible.
- The `permission.ask` hook is declared in the types and docs but is never called. A plugin cannot answer prompts
  itself, so learning has to go through a review step.
- The `config` hook may edit `agent.<name>.permission`; the rules end up after the built-in ones in the resolved
  agent (`opencode debug agent <name>` shows them). A permission set globally is appended after every agent's rules.
- `chat.params` reports the agent of each model call, including subagents. The utility agents `title`, `summary` and
  `compaction` share the session, so they must be ignored when tracking which agent a session belongs to. The v1 SDK
  types do not expose `agent` on sessions, but the runtime does (used as a fallback).
- Permission events are `permission.asked` / `permission.replied` at runtime, although the v1 SDK types still say
  `permission.updated`.
- Plugin tools can call `context.ask()` to raise a permission prompt. Agents start from `* allow`, so the plugin adds a
  global `readonly_guard_allow: ask` rule (evaluated after every agent's rules) to force the confirmation prompt.

**Plugin packaging (v1)**

- opencode treats every export of a plugin module as a plugin and calls it. Export only the default definition.
- A package is loaded from `exports["./server"]`, else `main`. A default export `{ id, server }` is supported since
  1.18.29. `engines.opencode` is enforced for npm packages only (one outside its range is skipped with a
  `session.error` event); a plugin loaded from a path runs whatever its range says. Peer dependencies such as
  `@opencode-ai/plugin` are installed for you.
- That install only happens for npm packages. A plugin loaded from a path (`file://…`) resolves its imports from that
  path, and if one fails (no `node_modules` there) opencode drops the plugin without a log line, even at `DEBUG`, while
  `opencode debug config` still lists it. This is why `dist/` is a bundle that only imports Node built-ins. The same
  goes for a checkout without `dist/` and for a `file://` path that does not exist: `opencode debug config` exits 0
  with nothing on stderr, and opencode starts as if nothing were wrong. A plugin that fails to import cannot report
  anything itself; only an outside check can (`opencode-readonly-guard doctor`).
- A plugin whose `server()` throws is dropped too, with one `failed to load plugin` line in opencode's log; an error
  in a `config` hook is logged (`plugin config hook failed`) and opencode goes on. Either way the agents keep whatever
  the config holds at that point, which is why this plugin carries a copy of its rule files, catches its own errors
  and fails closed.
- A toast sent while opencode starts (from `server()` or a `config` hook, without awaiting it: the request waits for
  the instance being started) reaches clients listening to the global event stream, which the TUI does.
- Plugin entries are merged only when they name the same `file://` URL or npm package (the last one is kept). Two
  specs of the same plugin load two copies of its module. Each gets the same input object, every `server()` runs
  before any `config` hook, global entries before project ones, and `hooks.tool` is read after all of them, which is
  what lets the copies agree on one of them.
- opencode 2.x plugins are `Plugin.define({ id, setup })`, V1 plugins do not run there, and V2 has a real
  `permission.hook("evaluate")` that would remove most of these workarounds.

**Models and tooling**

- Models in plan mode often refuse to run a write command to "test" the guard, because of the reminder. To exercise
  it, delegate to `explore` from `build`, or use an `edit: deny` harness agent (see the e2e tests).
- The rtk plugin rewrites commands (`ls` → `rtk ls`) before permissions are evaluated, so patterns must match the
  rewritten form (the allowlist has `rtk …` entries). Models then see a command they did not write and retry it
  several times, which wastes tokens (observed with Haiku and Sonnet).
- When spawning `opencode run` from another program, set `PWD` to the working directory (opencode trusts it over the
  real cwd; a mismatch fails with an `UnknownError`).

## Development

Everything is managed with [mise](https://mise.jdx.dev); Git hooks with [hk](https://hk.jdx.dev).

```sh
mise install                # bun, node, hk, actionlint, shellcheck and the pinned opencode
mise run setup              # bun install + git hooks (prettier, oxlint, tsc, conventional commits)
mise run check              # lint, formatting, types, unit tests (what CI runs)
mise run test:integration   # builds, then drives the real opencode without a model, and a packed tarball
mise run test:e2e           # opt-in, real model: E2E_MODEL=anthropic/claude-haiku-5-5
mise tasks                  # all tasks
```

The repository's own `opencode.json` loads the plugin from the checkout's `dist/` (`"plugin": ["."]`), so opencode
sessions started in a checkout or worktree are guarded by its build, work in progress included. Until
`mise run build` has run there, the entry is skipped without a word and a global install, if any, guards instead;
`bun src/cli.ts doctor` says which copy is in charge. [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) ("Hazards") explains what a build
changes for running and new sessions.

Code style follows opencode: TypeScript (strict, NodeNext), no semicolons, 120 columns, oxlint, prettier. See
[CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for adding rules and test cases.

# Session transcripts

Redacted transcripts of the maintainer's orchestration and work sessions with coding agents. They are history, not
documentation: they record what was tried and decided at the time, and may be wrong or superseded.
[README.md](../../README.md), [AGENTS.md](../../AGENTS.md), [CONTRIBUTING.md](../../CONTRIBUTING.md) and the code are
the source of truth.

## Naming

`YYYYMMDDHHMM-<slug>.md`: the start of the session, then a short lowercase slug with hyphens.

A session that is exported again after it went on (a long-running session, above all one that was compacted) gets
additional files, never a rewritten one: `YYYYMMDDHHMM-<slug>-p02.md`, `-p03.md`, and so on. The first file is part 1.
See "Continued sessions".

## Adding a transcript

1. Export the session with the fleet's session exporter (`export.py`, without `--sanitize`: that option replaces the
   whole content with placeholders), with `--out-dir` pointing to a directory of mode `0700` under
   `.state/<agent>/tmp/` (`install -d -m 0700 .state/<agent>/tmp/export`), never to this repository.
2. Redact it with the fleet's redactor in its `public` profile, for example
   `python3 ~/.config/nvim/scripts/session_redact.py --profile public < raw.md > memory/sessions/<name>.md`.
3. Run the redactor with `--check` from the repository root. It reads `.session-redact.toml` (settings only, no term)
   and exits 1 if anything is left in `memory/sessions/*.md`. This gate is local: the terms it uses are private, so CI
   cannot run it.
4. The maintainer reads the redacted file before it is committed.

The redactor hides names, not content: the text of a private repository's files that a tool printed into the session
goes through unchanged once the repository's name is hidden. Keep such output out of sessions you mean to publish, or
drop it from the export before step 2.

## Continued sessions: a re-export never overwrites a previous one

A published transcript is history: it is never rewritten, whether the session was compacted or not. When the same
session is exported again:

- find its latest part by the `**Session ID:**` line and the `<!-- session-export: through msg_... -->` marker in the
  first lines of the files;
- export from that marker with the exporter's `--since msg_...` (the bound is inclusive: the increment starts with the
  message of the marker) into the scratch directory, and name the result as the next part (`-pNN`);
- if the marker is already the newest message of the session, there is nothing to export;
- never use the exporter's `--force`, and never redirect redacted output over an existing file.

Each part is redacted and read like any other transcript, and carries the marker for the part after it.

## Why raw exports are never committed

A raw export holds what the redactor removes: secrets, private repository and host names, addresses, local paths and
personal data. The repository is public and Git history cannot be unpublished, so the only file that may reach a commit
is the redacted one. Delete raw exports once the redacted file is accepted; `.state/` and `.tmp/` are ignored by Git.

## Tooling

This directory is left alone by prettier and by the whitespace and newline hooks: a transcript keeps what the tools
printed, trailing spaces and very long lines included. The private key and merge conflict checks still apply. The npm
package publishes a whitelist of files (`files` in `package.json`) that does not include `memory/`.

# Contributing

Thanks for helping to make read-only agents trustworthy. The most useful contributions are **rules**: commands that
are safe to run without asking, flags that make a safe command unsafe, and test cases that pin the behaviour down.

## Setup

```sh
mise install        # bun, node, hk, actionlint, shellcheck, opencode (pinned in mise.toml)
mise run setup      # bun install + git hooks
mise run check      # what CI runs: lint, format, types, unit tests
```

Without mise you need Bun 1.4+, Node 22+ and `bun install`; `bun run check` does the same as `mise run check`.

## The shared rules

Everything the plugin decides on its own comes from the JSON files in [`rules/`](rules). They are editor-validated by
the JSON Schemas in [`rules/schema/`](rules/schema) and checked by the unit tests.

| File            | Contents                                                                                         |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `allow.json`    | opencode bash patterns that read-only agents may run without a prompt. Each has a `reason`.      |
| `ask.json`      | patterns that always ask, even when allowed above: flags that write files or run other programs. |
| `commands.json` | classification used by the write guard and the learning safety check (see below).                |
| `cases.json`    | expected verdicts for commands (`allow` / `ask` / `block`) and for patterns (`ok` true / false). |

Pattern syntax is opencode's: `*` matches anything, `?` one character, and a trailing ` *` also matches the bare
command. The **last matching rule wins**, which is why `ask.json` is applied after every allow rule (only the exact
`--help` commands of the help layer and the `2>&1` / `2>/dev/null` twins of exact rules follow it, both generated).
An exact rule therefore also covers its command followed by `2>&1` or `2>/dev/null`; do not add those by hand.

### Adding a command to the allowlist

An allow rule must be safe in **every** use the pattern can match, not just the common one.

1. Look for options that write files, delete, or run other programs (`--output`, `-o FILE`, `-exec`, `--pre`, `-x`,
   `-i`, `--in-place`, `-delete`, …), and for operands that do (`uniq IN OUT`, `date MMDDhhmm`, `hostname NAME`). If
   any exists, either do not allow the command, or add the dangerous option to `ask.json` (a prompt) and, if it is
   unambiguous, to the analyzer in `src/analyze.ts` (a block). Remember that GNU tools and git accept any unambiguous
   abbreviation of a long option (`sort --out=f`, `git branch --edit-desc`) and bundled short options (`-uo f`): the
   analyzer must catch those, and an `ask.json` glob should start from the shortest accepted prefix
   (`sort *--co*` for `--compress-program`).
2. Add the pattern and a short `reason` to `allow.json`. Use `cmd *` for "any arguments", `cmd sub*` for a family of
   subcommands, and the exact text for a single use. When the bare subcommand writes (`git branch NAME`,
   `mise settings KEY VALUE`), allow only the exact listing and the forms that cannot write (`git branch -a *`), and
   check the program's own behaviour: `git branch -v NAME` creates a branch, `git branch -a NAME` is refused.
3. If the command is reached through the rtk plugin (`rtk rewrite '<command>'` shows it), add the `rtk …` form too; a
   unit test checks this for the commands rtk rewrites.
4. Add cases to `cases.json`: at least one `allow`, plus an `ask` or `block` case for each dangerous option.
5. Run `mise run check`.

Other files:

- **`commands.json` → `hardWrite`:** commands that modify files whatever their arguments. They are blocked.
- **`commands.json` → `packageManagers`, `git`:** which subcommands write, and which git subcommands may get a
  wildcard rule from `/guard-review`.
- **`commands.json` → `herdr`:** `help` (printed help, allowed only as exact commands), `read` (read-only
  subcommands, a wildcard may follow), `ui` (what the `herdr-ui` preset in `src/sources.ts` allows inside herdr;
  never in `allow.json`) and `write` (blocked). Any other herdr subcommand must be added to `ask.json` as `herdr <sub> *`;
  there is no catch-all, because a `herdr *` ask rule would also silence the allowed reads. Keep the four lists
  disjoint and `allow.json` in step with `help` and `read` (the unit tests check both).
- **`commands.json` → `environment`:** `exportSafe`, the variables that may be exported or assigned because they only
  select a language, a format or turn a behaviour off, whatever their value (`LC_*` is a prefix); and `alwaysExported`,
  the variables the guard treats as exported even when the plugin's own environment lacks them. opencode never prompts
  for `export`, `declare` or a bare `NAME=value`, so only add a variable to `exportSafe` if no value of it can make a
  later command run or write something.
- **`commands.json` → `containers`:** the docker and podman `read` paths (`allow.json` must have
  `<engine> <path> *` for each, the unit tests check it) and the `write` paths the guard blocks. Allow rules start
  with the subcommand, so global options that pick another daemon (`-H`, `--context`) never match them.
- **`commands.json` → `subcommandHelp`:** extra git subcommands, and npm and mise subcommand paths, whose exact
  `<program> <subcommand> --help` is allowed by the help layer, after `ask.json` (git also gets `git.write` and
  `git.read`, herdr its `read` and `write` paths and its `herdr <path> *` ask rules; git, npm and mise get the `rtk`
  form, and git `git help <subcommand>`). The write guard treats a sole trailing `--help` after the subcommand path
  as a help request. The unit tests check that every derived command is allowed and that none matches an ask-listed
  flag.
- **`commands.json` → `wildcardSafe`:** commands for which `/guard-review` may offer `cmd *`. Only add a command whose
  every read-only use is harmless and whose write options are covered by `ask.json` or the analyzer.

Behaviour that depends on arguments (`tee`, `sed -i`, `find -exec`, `curl -o`, `git branch <name>`, …) lives in
`src/analyze.ts`, and for system tools with their own option rules (`systemctl`, `journalctl`, `ip`, `pacman`,
`docker`/`podman`, `virsh`, `lspci`, `ss`, `xxd`, `ps`) in `src/programs.ts`; add a unit test in
`test/unit/analyze.test.ts` and a case in
`cases.json`. Check the program's real behaviour (its sources, or a run against a scratch target such as
`virsh -c test:///default`) rather than its manual alone.

## Tests

| Tier        | Command                     | Needs                                    |
| ----------- | --------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| unit        | `mise run test`             | nothing                                  |
| integration | `mise run test:integration` | opencode on `PATH`; builds `dist/` first |
| e2e         | `mise run test:e2e`         | opencode credentials; costs a few cents  |

Unit tests include every case in `cases.json`, so a rule change is tested by adding a line there. Integration tests
load the built plugin (and a packed tarball) into the real opencode without calling a model. The e2e tests are
opt-in because they use a real model.

## Commits and pull requests

- [Conventional Commits](https://www.conventionalcommits.org), enforced by the `commit-msg` hook: `feat(rules): …`,
  `fix(analyze): …`, `docs: …`, `test: …`, `build: …`, `ci: …`, `chore: …`.
- One logical change per commit. A rule change and its `cases.json` entries go together.
- Update `CHANGELOG.md` for user-visible changes.
- The pre-commit hook (hk) runs prettier, oxlint, tsc, actionlint and whitespace checks; CI runs the same plus the
  tests. Please run `mise run check` before pushing.
- Agents' scratch files, state and the redacted session transcripts in `memory/sessions/` follow the conventions in
  [AGENTS.md](AGENTS.md) ("State, scratch and transcripts"); contributors can ignore them.

## Dependency updates

[Renovate](https://docs.renovatebot.com) (`renovate.json`) opens the update pull requests once a week: npm packages
with `bun.lock`, the tools in `mise.toml`, the hk version in `hk.pkl`, and the GitHub Actions, pinned to commit SHAs.
Minor and patch updates are grouped into one pull request, majors come one by one, Actions have their own group, and
commits are `build(deps): …` or `ci(deps): …`. The supported ranges (`peerDependencies`, `engines`) are left alone.

opencode (`aqua:anomalyco/opencode` in `mise.toml`) and `@opencode-ai/plugin` come together in an "opencode" pull
request and stay below 2.0. CI runs the integration tests against the new version; run `mise run test:integration`
locally as well before merging, and update "Tested with opencode …" in the README once it passes.

## Reporting a bypass

If a command writes from a read-only agent without being blocked or asked about, open an issue with the command, the
agent, and the opencode version. Add it to [`rules/cases.json`](rules/cases.json) as a failing case if you can.

## Statements, redirections and environment prefixes

Design note: pull request `docs/env-prefix-design`. opencode builds one pattern per tree-sitter `command` node: the
text includes the redirections of that command (`herdr --help 2>&1`); `cd`, `pushd` and `popd` are skipped;
declarations (`export`, `local`, …), bare assignments (`B=/x`), `[ ]`, `[[ ]]` and `(( ))` are not command nodes, so
they never prompt (the write guard judges them since the exported-variables fix).

Done with globs (PR 1.4 `feat/rules-utilities`):

- [x] Builtins that prompt but run nothing: `shift *`, `continue *`, `break *`, `true *`, `false *`, `read *` (the

  - [ ] `:` (`: ${X:=v}`) still asks: allow patterns must start with a letter (`rules.test.ts`), and `:` is not worth
        an exception.
- [x] `2>&1` and `2>/dev/null` twins of every exact allowed command, generated in `src/rules.ts` after the help layer.

      (`export -p`, `declare`), which opencode never prompts for.
  - [ ] A pattern in a later `case` clause (`b) cmd ;;`) is still taken for a command, so `check` asks for `case`

1: # opencode-readonly-guard
2: 
3: Make opencode's read-only agents (`plan`, `explore`, and any agent with `edit: deny`) actually read-only.
4: 
5: In opencode, "plan mode" is a request to the model, not a restriction: the `plan` and `explore` agents can run any
6: shell command, so a model that ignores the reminder can still `rm`, `sed -i` or `> file`. This plugin closes that gap:
7: 
8: - **Write guard.** Before opencode evaluates any permission rule, the full command line is parsed and refused if it
9:   writes: redirections in any position, `tee` to a file, `rm`/`cp`/`mv`/…, `sed -i`, `git commit`, `npm install`,
10:   `find -delete`, `curl -o`, and wrappers around them (`sudo`, `env`, `xargs`, `bash -c`, `$(…)`). The model gets an
11:   error that tells it to return the data in its reply instead.
12: - **Shared allowlist.** Read-only agents ask before running anything except a vetted list of read-only commands
13:   (`ls`, `cat`, `rg`, `git log`, `herdr agent list`, …). The list lives in [`rules/`](rules) as plain JSON that anyone
14:   can extend.
15: - **Reviewed learning.** An "always" answer in a read-only agent is only logged as a candidate. `/guard-review` shows
16:   candidates with safe pattern options, and a rule is added only after you confirm the exact pattern.
17: - **Event log.** Every shell command, block, prompt and answer in a read-only agent is recorded, so the policy can be
18:   improved with data.
19: 
20: Tested with opencode 1.19.3 (supported range `>=1.18.29 <2`). opencode 2.x has a different plugin API and is not
21: supported yet, see [TODO.md](TODO.md).

---
title: CLI reference
description: Herdr commands for sessions, workspaces, tabs, panes, notifications, agents, waits, integrations, and status.
---

Herdr’s CLI talks to the running server over the same local socket API used by integrations and agents.

Most commands print JSON responses for deterministic automation in scripts.

## Launch and status

```bash
herdr                         # launch or attach to the default session
herdr --remote workbox        # attach through SSH, using local keybindings
herdr --default-config        # print default config
herdr update                  # download and install from the configured channel
herdr completion zsh          # generate a zsh completion script
herdr channel show            # print stable or preview
herdr channel set preview     # opt into preview builds
herdr channel set stable      # return a direct install to stable
herdr --version               # print version
```

Optional launch and update settings:

- Add `--session <name>` to use a named session instead of the default.
- Add `--remote-keybindings server` to remote attach to use server keybindings instead of local ones.
- Experimental live handoff requires explicit `--handoff` on `herdr --remote` or `herdr update`. It is not the normal setup or connection path; see [Updates](/docs/install/#update).

Status commands:

```bash
herdr status
herdr status server
herdr status client
```

API schema commands:

```bash
herdr api schema
herdr api schema --json
herdr api schema --output herdr-api.schema.json
```

`herdr api schema` prints a short summary of the socket protocol schema bundled
with the installed binary. Use `--json` for the full JSON Schema document, or
`--output PATH` to write that document to a file.

## Saved SSH machines

```bash
herdr machine list
herdr machine add workbox
herdr machine add workbox --label "Build machine"
herdr machine rename <profile-id> --label "New name"
herdr machine disable <profile-id>
herdr machine enable <profile-id>
herdr machine remove <profile-id>
```

In an interactive terminal, `machine add` discovers running sessions and lets you choose when several are running. No running sessions, or no Herdr installation, uses `default`; failed queries against an installed binary require an explicit choice. Add `--remote-session <name>` to skip discovery. Non-interactive commands use `default` unless that flag is supplied. `machine list` accepts optional `--json` for scripts. See [Connecting machines](/docs/connecting-machines/) for the full setup and connection guide.

`machine add` checks the remote installation's capabilities, installs or updates with approval only when needed, and starts the requested session's background server before saving. Compatible release versions do not need to match. Run setup in an interactive terminal when installation or restart approval is required; failed or cancelled setup does not save a profile. Replacing a running server requires explicit approval with a default answer of No, and stops its pane processes. `machine add` never enables experimental handoff implicitly.

Changes apply automatically to open local Herdr clients, normally within a second. Added or enabled machines connect in the background; renaming does not reconnect. Removing or disabling disconnects only that machine and leaves its remote sessions running. Removing the machine you are viewing returns to Local, or shows Local as unavailable until it reconnects. Each profile stores an opaque ID, label, SSH target, explicit remote session, and enabled state in client state. Herdr does not store passwords, private keys, or other SSH credentials.

Use `herdr machine status [<label-or-id>] [--json]` for fresh, noninteractive SSH and remote Herdr checks. `reachable` describes this check, not a TUI's current connection. Use `herdr machine reconnect <label-or-id>` in a terminal for SSH authentication and verification; it does not install or update Herdr. Open clients retry failed connections within 30 seconds. Clicking `! auth` or `! error` shows the latest error and CLI guidance; collapsed sidebars show `!`. See [Recovering SSH authentication](/docs/connecting-machines/#recovering-ssh-authentication) for platform limits. For remote setup, use `herdr --remote workbox`, adding `--session <name>` only for a named session.

Workspace, tab, pane IDs, and agent names belong to a single server. Selecting a machine in the UI does not retarget CLI commands. Use the global **prefix** `--machine <label-or-id>` to route API commands to a saved SSH machine:

```bash
herdr --machine "Build machine" agent list
herdr --machine <profile-id> pane list
herdr --machine "Build machine" agent prompt w1:p1 "review this change"
herdr --machine "Build machine" worktree create --cwd /srv/project --branch review
```

The selector must match an enabled saved profile ID or a unique, case-sensitive label, not an arbitrary SSH hostname. The saved remote session is used; combining `--machine` with `--session` or `--remote` is an error. Without the prefix, commands retain their existing local session/socket behavior.

Supported commands are `workspace`, `worktree`, `tab`, `pane`, `notification`, `agent` (except `attach` and local `explain --file`), `api snapshot`, `status server`, and API-backed plugin commands (`link`, `unlink`, `enable`, `disable`, `list`, `action`, `log`, `pane`). Server commands support `stop`, `reload-config`, `agent-manifests`, and `reload-agent-manifests`. Local installation/configuration commands, plugin installation, session management, and interactive terminal attachment are not forwarded.

Requests and responses travel through the JSON API over non-interactive SSH; API payloads are not interpolated into the SSH shell command. No open TUI is required, and the bridge never installs, starts, or restarts a server. Update the local CLI and remote Herdr installation to support machine forwarding, and keep the running remote server's API protocol compatible. Authentication, unavailable machines, and incompatible versions fail without falling back to Local. Requests are not automatically retried after connection failure.

Local pane IDs are not inherited by remote commands. Use explicit remote IDs; `--current` cannot refer to the caller's local pane. Remote worktree paths must be absolute, `~`, or start with `~/` (expanded on the server); plugin link paths must be absolute. The prefix targets one machine at a time; combined listings and routing through another TUI's connections are not included.

## Shell completions

```bash
herdr completion zsh
herdr completions zsh
herdr completion bash
herdr completion fish
herdr completion powershell
herdr completion elvish
```

`completion` prints the script to stdout. `completions` is an alias. For a
temporary zsh session, load the script directly:

```bash
source <(herdr completion zsh)
```

For a persistent zsh setup, write the generated `_herdr` function somewhere on
your `fpath` before `compinit` runs:

```bash
mkdir -p ~/.zfunc
herdr completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_herdr
```

Then make sure your `.zshrc` contains:

```zsh
fpath=(~/.zfunc $fpath)
autoload -Uz compinit
compinit
```

## Server

```bash
herdr server
herdr server stop
herdr server reload-config
herdr server agent-manifests [--json]
herdr server update-agent-manifests [--json]
herdr server reload-agent-manifests
```

`herdr server` runs the headless server explicitly. Use it for supervised or service-style setups. `reload-config` applies reloadable settings without restarting panes. `agent-manifests` shows the active agent detection manifest sources, cached remote versions, and last remote update results. `update-agent-manifests` fetches remote manifest updates immediately, reloads them into the running server, and prints the updated manifest status; pass `--json` for the raw status response. `reload-agent-manifests` reloads agent detection manifests into the running server after local override edits.

## Notifications

```bash
herdr notification show <title> [--body TEXT] [--position top-left|top-right|bottom-left|bottom-right] [--sound none|done|request]
```

`notification show` uses the configured `[ui.toast]` delivery. `--position` only affects in-app Herdr toasts. `--sound` defaults to `none`; `done` and `request` play the existing finished and needs-attention sounds only when the notification is shown.

## Sessions

```bash
herdr session list [--json]
herdr session attach <name>
herdr session stop <name> [--json]
herdr session delete <name> [--json]
```

Use `default` as the session name when you need to stop the default session explicitly.

## Workspaces

```bash
herdr workspace list
herdr workspace create [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]
herdr workspace get <workspace_id>
herdr workspace focus <workspace_id>
herdr workspace rename <workspace_id> <label>
herdr workspace report-metadata <workspace_id> --source ID [--token NAME=VALUE] [--clear-token NAME] [--seq N] [--ttl-ms N]
herdr workspace close <workspace_id> [--group]
```

Create a workspace without stealing focus:

```bash
herdr workspace create --cwd ~/project --label api --no-focus
```

A workspace is a top-level project or work context. Creating one also creates its first tab and root pane. The JSON response exposes their IDs as `.result.workspace.workspace_id`, `.result.tab.tab_id`, and `.result.root_pane.pane_id`.

## Worktrees

```bash
herdr worktree list [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] [--trust-repository]
herdr worktree create [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] [--branch NAME] [--base REF] [--path PATH] [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus] [--trust-repository]
herdr worktree open [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] (--path PATH | --branch NAME) [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus] [--trust-repository]
herdr worktree remove --workspace ID [--force] [--trust-repository]
```

Worktrees are normal Herdr workspaces with Git checkout provenance. `worktree create` creates a Git worktree checkout, opens it as a workspace, and groups it with the parent repo workspace. If `--branch` names an existing local branch, Herdr checks it out; otherwise it creates the branch from `--base` or `HEAD`. Without `--path`, Herdr creates the checkout under `<worktrees.directory>/<repo>/<branch-slug>`.

`workspace close` closes only Herdr state. Closing a primary workspace while linked-worktree workspaces are open requires `--group`; without it, the command leaves the group open and returns `workspace_group_close_required`. To delete the checkout, run `worktree remove`. It runs `git worktree remove`, never deletes the branch, and requires `--force` when Git refuses a dirty checkout.

Git rejects repositories owned by another user by default. If you have independently verified the repository, pass `--trust-repository` to trust its resolved path for that command only. Herdr does not change your Git configuration.

## Tabs

```bash
herdr tab list [--workspace <workspace_id>]
herdr tab create [--workspace <workspace_id>] [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]
herdr tab get <tab_id>
herdr tab focus <tab_id>
herdr tab rename <tab_id> <label>
herdr tab close <tab_id>
```

A tab is another terminal layout inside a workspace. Without `--workspace`, `tab create` uses the active workspace and fails if none exists. Its JSON response exposes `.result.tab.tab_id` and `.result.root_pane.pane_id`. Closing a workspace's last tab also closes the workspace, matching the TUI close-tab action. If `confirm_close` is enabled and closing the tab would also close a whole worktree group, `tab close` returns a `confirmation_required` error instead.

With `ui.confirm_close` enabled, the TUI asks for confirmation before closing a workspace's last tab or its only pane from a keybinding or the tab/pane menu. Ordinary pane closes and CLI/API closes remain immediate.

Workspace and tab creation, and pane splitting, leave focus unchanged by default. `--focus` selects the new layout; `--no-focus` states the default explicitly. Without `--cwd`, new terminals follow the configured `terminal.new_cwd` policy, which follows the source pane or workspace by default. Each `--env KEY=VALUE` adds or replaces that variable in the new root shell.

Summary of herdr v0.9.5 docs on worktrees, plus tab/workspace options and session restore.

**Worktree CLI (cli-reference.mdx, "Worktrees" section)**
- `herdr worktree list [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] [--trust-repository]`
- `herdr worktree create [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] [--branch NAME] [--base REF] [--path PATH] [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus] [--trust-repository]`
- `herdr worktree open [--workspace ID | --cwd PATH] (--path PATH | --branch NAME) [--label TEXT] [--focus] [--no-focus] [--trust-repository]`
- `herdr worktree remove --workspace ID [--force] [--trust-repository]`
- Quote: "Worktrees are normal Herdr workspaces with Git checkout provenance." `create` makes the Git worktree checkout, opens it as a workspace, and "groups it with the parent repo workspace".
- Branch naming: if `--branch` names an existing local branch, Herdr checks it out. Otherwise it creates the branch from `--base`, or from `HEAD` if `--base` is absent.
- Checkout location: without `--path`, the checkout goes under `<worktrees.directory>/<repo>/<branch-slug>`.
- Config key `worktrees.directory`: type string, default `"~/.herdr/worktrees"`. Its description is "Root directory under which Herdr creates <repo>/<branch-slug> checkouts." It is the only worktree location key. Section id is `worktrees`.
- `worktree remove` runs `git worktree remove`, "never deletes the branch", and needs `--force` when Git refuses a dirty checkout.
- `workspace close` "closes only Herdr state" and leaves the checkout on disk. Deleting the checkout requires `worktree remove`.
- Group close: closing a primary workspace while linked-worktree workspaces are open needs `--group`. Without it, the group stays open and the command returns the error `workspace_group_close_required`.
- `tab close`: if `ui.confirm_close` is on and closing the tab would close a whole worktree group, it returns a `confirmation_required` error.
- `--trust-repository`: Git rejects repositories owned by another user by default. The flag trusts the resolved path "for that command only", and Herdr does not change your Git config.
- Remote use: `herdr --machine "Build machine" worktree create --cwd /srv/project --branch review`. Remote worktree paths must be absolute, `~`, or start with `~/`, and are expanded on the server.
- Plugins: the plugin example `ogulcancelik/herdr-plugin-examples/worktree-bootstrap` is mentioned as an install example.

**Worktree keybindings and sidebar (config-reference.json)**
- `keys.new_worktree` defaults to `"prefix+shift+g"` ("Create a Git worktree from the selected workspace").
- `keys.open_worktree` is unset by default.
- `keys.remove_worktree` is unset by default. Description: "Delete the selected managed worktree checkout after confirmation."
- `ui.sidebar.spaces.row_gap` defaults to `0`. It sets "Blank terminal rows between worktree groups and unrelated top-level Spaces. Worktree parents and their indented children remain packed."
- So linked worktrees appear in the sidebar's Space list as indented children under their parent repo workspace.
- `ui.sidebar.spaces.rows` defaults to `[["state_icon", "workspace"], ["branch", "git_status"]]`, which shows the branch and git status per Space.
- `ui.confirm_close` defaults to `true`.

**`herdr workspace create`**
- `herdr workspace create [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]`
- It also creates the first tab and root pane. The response has `.result.workspace.workspace_id`, `.result.tab.tab_id` and `.result.root_pane.pane_id`.
- Related commands: `workspace list|get|focus|rename|report-metadata`, and `workspace close <id> [--group]`.

**`herdr tab create`**
- `herdr tab create [--workspace <workspace_id>] [--cwd PATH] [--label TEXT] [--env KEY=VALUE] [--focus] [--no-focus]`
- Without `--workspace` it uses the active workspace and fails if none exists.
- The response has `.result.tab` and `.result.root_pane`.
- Focus is unchanged by default. `--focus` selects the new layout, and `--no-focus` states the default explicitly.
- Without `--cwd`, the `terminal.new_cwd` policy applies: values `follow` (default), `home`, `current`, `path`.
- Each `--env` adds or replaces a variable in the new root shell. It can be repeated.
- The `ui.prompt_new_tab_name` default is `true`. It applies only to the TUI.

**Session restore (session-state.mdx)**
- Yes, opencode agents are resumed after a server restart, subject to conditions below.
- Native agent session restore is on by default. Setting `[session] resume_agents_on_restore = false` disables it.
- OpenCode needs integration version `5` or newer. The resume command is `opencode --session <id>`. Run `herdr integration install opencode` and `herdr integration status` to check.
- Only panes that reported a native session reference through an official integration, or whose agent reported its own resume command, are resumed.
- Unsupported, missing, invalid, duplicated or stale references restore as plain shells in the saved cwd.
- Resume happens after a client attaches and provides terminal size and theme. Eligible panes across all workspaces and tabs resume without needing focus.
- `session.startup_per_agent_delay_ms` defaults to `100`. It spaces automatic restores, and the first agent starts without the delay.
- Server restart does not keep processes running. It restores workspaces, tabs, panes, cwd, layout and focus. Recent screen content returns only if `[experimental] pane_history = true`, which is off by default.
- Detach and reattach keeps everything running.
- Resume commands run only for `agent start` kinds or hooks that report them. `pane report-agent` takes `-- RESUME_COMMAND...`. The first argument must be a plain command on `PATH`, and no argument may contain an apostrophe.

-   `aqua` packages with `http` [package type](https://aquaproj.github.io/docs/reference/registry-config/#package-types). However if the short name using `aqua` backend is supported by Renovate, it will be updated. e.g. [`aqua:helm/helm`](https://github.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry/blob/main/pkgs/helm/helm/registry.yaml) is not supported, but `helm` or `aqua:helm` is supported.
    
-   `aqua` packages with [`version_filter`](https://aquaproj.github.io/docs/reference/registry-config/version-prefix). We don't read the aqua registry itself, so we can't support this feature. If some packages using `version_filter` like [`aqua:biomejs/biome`](https://github.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry/blob/main/pkgs/biomejs/biome/registry.yaml) are not updated or updated incorrectly, set `extractVersion` in the Renovate config manually like below.
    
    `{   "packageRules": [     {       "matchDepNames": ["aqua:biomejs/biome"],       "extractVersion": "cli/(?<version>.+)"     }   ] }`
    
-   Some of `ubi` backend tools with [`tag_regex`](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/backends/ubi.html#ubi-uses-weird-versions) option. The `tag_regex` option is used as `extractVersion`, but the regex engines are not the same between mise and Renovate. If the version is not updated or updated incorrectly, override `extractVersion` manually in the Renovate config.
    
-   Some of `github` backend tools with [`version_prefix`](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/backends/github.html) option. The `version_prefix` option is converted to `extractVersion` by escaping special regex characters. If the version is not updated or updated incorrectly, override `extractVersion` manually in the Renovate config.
    
-   Renovate will prefer the `github:` backend over other backends, if using the tool definition from the mise registry

28: Pattern syntax is opencode's: `*` matches anything, `?` one character, and a trailing ` *` also matches the bare
29: command. The **last matching rule wins**, which is why `ask.json` is applied after every allow rule (only the exact
30: `--help` commands of the help layer follow it).
31: 
32: ### Adding a command to the allowlist
33: 
34: An allow rule must be safe in **every** use the pattern can match, not just the common one.
35: 
36: 1. Look for options that write files, delete, or run other programs (`--output`, `-o FILE`, `-exec`, `--pre`, `-x`,
37:    `-i`, `--in-place`, `-delete`, …), and for operands that do (`uniq IN OUT`, `date MMDDhhmm`, `hostname NAME`). If
38:    any exists, either do not allow the command, or add the dangerous option to `ask.json` (a prompt) and, if it is
39:    unambiguous, to the analyzer in `src/analyze.ts` (a block). Remember that GNU tools and git accept any unambiguous
40:    abbreviation of a long option (`sort --out=f`, `git branch --edit-desc`) and bundled short options (`-uo f`): the
41:    analyzer must catch those, and an `ask.json` glob should start from the shortest accepted prefix
42:    (`sort *--co*` for `--compress-program`).
43: 2. Add the pattern and a short `reason` to `allow.json`. Use `cmd *` for "any arguments", `cmd sub*` for a family of
44:    subcommands, and the exact text for a single use. When the bare subcommand writes (`git branch NAME`,
45:    `mise settings KEY VALUE`), allow only the exact listing and the forms that cannot write (`git branch -a *`), and
46:    check the program's own behaviour: `git branch -v NAME` creates a branch, `git branch -a NAME` is refused.
47: 3. If the command is reached through the rtk plugin (`rtk rewrite '<command>'` shows it), add the `rtk …` form too; a
48:    unit test checks this for the commands rtk rewrites.

50: 5. Run `mise run check`.
